column3: Its exact formula shows that accumulated earnings do not protect a people once the consequence arrives.
The book comes after earlier generations were destroyed, preserving their fate as a warning beyond former prosperity.
Brief worldly enjoyment followed by Hell echoes the focus's contrast between temporary benefit and final outcome.
Its repeated formula directly states that what earlier people earned did not avail them.
It begins the immediate sequence: denial persists until the painful punishment is seen.
Self-sufficiency frames the false security that the focus shows to be ineffective at the end.
Wealth and earnings explicitly fail to avail their owner, closely matching the focus's claim.
The next ayah explains that no town was destroyed without prior warners.
A supposed shelter that gives no protection offers a limited parallel to benefit proving useless.
The speaker's wealth explicitly fails him at judgment, a direct personal counterpart to the focus.
The destruction of earlier counterparts supplies a precedent for the threatened people after warning.
Earlier peoples enjoyed greater strength and wealth, yet their works came to nothing and they lost.
Granted faculties and power did not avail a people when they denied God's signs.
The punishment's sudden arrival is the immediate event that makes prior enjoyment useless.
Wealth and children cannot avail disbelievers against God, directly expressing failed worldly security.
Earlier peoples' greater power and accomplishments did not avail them when their end came.
It completes the local explanation: destruction followed warning and was not unjust.
Gathered numbers and pride fail to avail their possessors, paralleling the focus's failed resources.
At return each soul faces what it sent ahead, while its fabricated supports vanish.
The promised punishment is not broken by its apparent delay, clarifying the years before the focus's outcome.
God's independence after people reject messengers does not develop their temporary enjoyment or its failure.
Enjoyment until a fixed time presents benefit as bounded rather than permanent security.
The desperate request for delay follows the sudden punishment in the focus's immediate sequence.
The wrongdoers' mutual alliances cannot avail against God, a social form of failed protection.
Thamud are told to enjoy themselves only until a specified time, closely matching limited respite.
The focus's preceding question explicitly poses prolonged enjoyment over years.
It contrasts temporary worldly enjoyment with the lasting promise and later compulsory appearance for judgment.
Worldly enjoyment is followed by return and severe punishment for disbelief.
Moses being chosen for God does not illuminate temporary enjoyment or the arrival of punishment.
Wealth cannot avail its owner at the moment of ruin, directly paralleling the focus.
The rhetorical mention of the Day of Recompense contains no specific link to enjoyment or its failure.
It is the immediate question about hastening the very punishment that follows the years of enjoyment.
All given things are worldly enjoyment and adornment, while what is with God is better and more lasting.
Provision for humans and livestock establishes ordinary benefit but not its limitation or final failure.
The promised event arriving after years is the direct antecedent to the focus's conclusion.
The command to enjoy disbelief only briefly joins present benefit to the coming punishment.
It identifies provision as sustenance, without connecting it to delayed judgment or uselessness.
The family's fear that persistent remembrance will exhaust Jacob does not concern enjoyment or punishment.
Conjecture cannot avail against truth, an abstract but different use of the failure-of-sufficiency pattern.
It asks whether disbelievers have been repaid for what they did, supplying the later accountability frame.
Affluent town leaders reject warning, linking prosperity to the resistance that precedes destruction.
Good enjoyment is granted only to an appointed term, while turning away brings fear of a great-day punishment.
False objects of invocation vanish and no escape remains, paralleling supports failing at the end.
The counting of years introduces the smallness of worldly duration, but not enjoyment's failure.
Food that neither nourishes nor relieves hunger is a narrow analogue of benefit that does not serve its purpose.
The loss of selves and vanished fabrications supplies only a general final-loss parallel.
People describe their earthly stay as a day or part of a day, reducing the apparent length of respite.
Disbelievers may receive brief worldly enjoyment before being compelled to the punishment of the Fire.
Their fabrications vanish from them, but the ayah does not develop worldly enjoyment or delay.
God declares the earthly stay to have been only a little, reframing long respite as brief.
The command to enjoy themselves is followed by certain knowledge, making enjoyment a limited reprieve.
The challenge about worshipping carved objects does not itself address temporary benefit or punishment.
A destroyed town cannot return, reinforcing the finality of the outcome after destruction.
The required divorce provision is a legal support rule unrelated to the focus's warning sequence.
The question about emitted semen has no material connection to temporary enjoyment or its end.
Towns are not destroyed until a messenger has recited signs to them, directly explaining the warning before judgment.
Provision and economic justice in the marriage context do not illuminate the focus's temporary-respite theme.
The oath by visible things contributes no discernible connection to enjoyment or punishment.
The rejection of a human warner relates broadly to the warning element before the threatened outcome.
Followers ask their leaders to remove part of the Fire, but no one can bear another's punishment.
False inventions vanish on the Day of surrender, a general image of failed supports at judgment.
The verse calls creation a reminder, with only a broad connection to the focus's warning function.
A year's maintenance for widows is a legal arrangement rather than worldly respite before punishment.
Punishment delayed for a counted term still arrives irresistibly, directly clarifying the focus's sequence.
Signs and warnings do not avail a people who refuse faith, connecting warning to ineffective reception.
Worldly enjoyment is followed by return to God and a report of people's deeds.
Associating partners makes previous works come to nothing, a general outcome without the enjoyment theme.
It directs opponents to await the precedent of earlier destructive days after warning.
The divorce gift is a legal duty and does not bear on temporary enjoyment or final consequence.
At judgment false claims vanish before God's truth, providing only a general final-exposure parallel.
The majestic Qur'an is a broad warning resource but has no specific relation to the focus's benefit-and-punishment contrast.
Human dependence on God counters self-sufficiency generally, without the focus's temporal sequence.
Jacob's prudent plan cannot avail against God, paralleling the limits of apparent protective means.
Prosperous towns that exulted in their livelihood were destroyed, leaving their dwellings desolate.
Being preoccupied on the Day does not use sufficiency in the sense of protection or benefit.
Reward for what people did offers a general accountability frame but not the focus's warning-respite pattern.
The destruction of Aad is paired with God's warnings, supplying a precedent for the threatened outcome.
Even angelic intercession cannot avail except by God's permission, directly denying independent protection.
The gods taken as means of nearness fail to help and vanish, paralleling useless supports at judgment.
The repeated question about punishment and warnings preserves the warning-then-consequence pattern.
The command to enjoy themselves amid ingratitude is followed by a future reckoning of knowledge.
When the foretold fulfillment comes, people seek intercession or return to act differently, but their fabrications have vanished.
The repeated question about punishment and warnings reinforces the fate awaiting persistent rejection.
God's enriching and contenting action concerns provision, not its failure at judgment.
Shuayb's deniers become as though they had never prospered there, a close destruction-after-prosperity parallel.
Destroyed unjust towns, abandoned wells, and lofty palaces make former prosperity visibly useless.
Practical precaution cannot avail against God, limiting the security attributed to human means.
Their final abode in Hell is repayment for what they used to earn, supplying accountability after conduct.
The Romans' defeat does not develop temporary enjoyment, warning, or the failure of worldly supports.
Worldly enjoyment is explicitly declared little when measured against the Hereafter.
The rebuke of faulty judgment has no particular connection to the focus's respite-and-punishment sequence.
Scattered dust does not identify worldly enjoyment, warning, or a failed means of protection.
God repays the best of what believers did, a general recompense theme without the focus's contrast.
Divine testing of hidden thoughts and destiny provides a remote accountability connection only.
The description of a lofty garden has no material link to temporary worldly enjoyment.
Repeated treaty breaking is unrelated to the focus's enjoyment-before-punishment structure.
God knows charitable acts in a legal instruction, but it does not address worldly benefit or final failure.
The statement of Satan's curse and intended share is unrelated to the focus.
God's knowledge of what is open and hidden does not develop the focus's temporary enjoyment theme.
Shuayb's earlier Madyan warning names the unjust conduct whose later destruction illustrates failed worldly security.
It warns against being deceived by disbelievers' movement and apparent success in the land.
Worldly life is explicitly called the enjoyment of delusion when measured against final recompense.
It declares worldly enjoyment little and the Hereafter better for those who are mindful.
After being reminded, people rejoice in opened worldly goods and are then seized suddenly in despair.
The worldly life has deceived those who take it as play, before their ultimate requital.
The jinn and humans reach the appointed term after benefiting from one another, showing benefit bounded by judgment.
Increased prosperity and ease are followed by an unexpected seizure when people misread their history.
It asks whether the people of towns feel secure from God's punishment coming by night.
It asks whether the people of towns feel secure from God's punishment coming in the morning.
It rejects feeling secure from God's plan, the presumption exposed by the focus's sudden outcome.
Wealth and children become a means of punishment in this world and end in disbelief, not security.
The parable of worldly life shows flourishing vegetation abruptly becoming stubble after people think they possess it.
The people of Jonah alone believed before punishment and were allowed enjoyment for a time.
Those seeking worldly life and its adornment receive their works here, setting up the contrast with the Hereafter.
Their worldly works become fruitless in the Hereafter, so present gain does not secure the final result.
Salih gives Thamud a specific three-day period of enjoyment before the unbroken promise arrives.
After hamstringing the she-camel, Thamud are told to enjoy their homes for three days before the cry seizes them.
Shuayb's rescue and the seizure of the wrongdoers provide the direct Madyan resolution to his warnings.
Madyan is destroyed as though it had never prospered there, closely matching 26:207's reversal.
Worldly life is described as only enjoyment compared with the Hereafter.
Punishment in this world and a greater punishment in the Hereafter leave no protector against God.
Those who prefer worldly life and turn from God's path are marked by that fatal preference.
The command to enjoy themselves is an ironic temporary allowance before their destination becomes known.
People are left to eat, enjoy themselves, and be diverted by hope until they come to know the consequence.
A little enjoyment is followed by painful punishment, directly stating the focus's temporal contrast.
Whoever seeks the immediate world receives a limited grant, then faces Hell blamed and rejected.
Both groups receive a worldly grant, showing that present provision is not itself final approval.
The parable introduces a man whose two productive gardens become the basis for false security.
The garden's wealth is destroyed, and its owner realizes that his resources and support cannot save him.
After the garden's ruin, he has no party to help him against God and cannot defend himself.
Worldly life is likened to vegetation that flourishes and then becomes scattered debris.
Wealth and children are worldly adornment, while enduring righteous deeds are better in lasting reward and hope.
Temporary worldly splendor is a test, while God's provision is better and more lasting.
God allowed the disbelievers and their fathers enjoyment until life grew long for them, directly paralleling years of respite.
The affluent leaders of a town reject their messenger, linking luxury to the refusal that brings destruction.
It challenges the assumption that wealth and children given to deniers are a hastening of good for them.
It completes the correction: they do not perceive the true meaning of their apparent abundance.
The false gods say that God allowed their worshippers and fathers enjoyment until they forgot the reminder and perished.
The people reject Shuayb and are seized by the punishment of the overshadowing day, resolving the local warning scene.
Hell already encompasses the disbelievers, showing that present delay does not remove the threatened end.
Worldly life is diversion and play, while the lasting life is the true life if people knew.
God gives disbelievers a little enjoyment and then drives them to a harsh punishment.
Wealth and children are claimed as immunity from punishment, directly presenting the false confidence refuted by the focus.
If God punished people for what they earned immediately none would remain, but He defers them to an appointed term.
Mercy grants enjoyment only until a time, explicitly defining provision as temporary.
God made earlier deniers taste disgrace in worldly life before the greater punishment of the Hereafter.
When messengers brought clear proofs, people rejoiced in their own knowledge until the punishment they mocked encompassed them.
The temporary worldly adornments of disbelievers are described as provisions of this life only.
Houses and furnishings are further examples of the transient luxury allotted in worldly life.
All such luxury is worldly enjoyment, while the Hereafter with God belongs to the mindful.
Disbelievers enjoy and eat for a time, but the Fire is their final lodging.
Worldly life is play and diversion, and its rewards should not be surrendered for it.
Worldly life flourishes, boasts, and multiplies before becoming dry debris, while the Hereafter contains punishment or forgiveness.
The owners of the garden plan to harvest its yield, introducing a prosperity that is about to be removed.
Their garden becomes as though already harvested after a destructive visitation, overturning expected enjoyment.
After the loss, they hope their Lord may replace the garden with something better, acknowledging dependence beyond possession.
Deniers are left in diversion until they meet the day they are promised.
At the Hour, people perceive their long stay as only an evening or its morning.
The preference for worldly life is contrasted with the better and more enduring Hereafter.
It states the Hereafter is better and more lasting, supplying the focus's decisive value contrast.
Rivalry in accumulation distracts people, exposing the futile pursuit behind apparent abundance.
That distraction continues until the graves are visited, bringing accumulation to its unavoidable end.
